description: Cluster 1 is the largest cluster, with 159 publications, and has had a presence since the inception of the journal. The primary focus of the cluster involves international business education, international business management, MBA, foreign language and Globalization (Crittenden and Wilson 2006; Kedia, Harveston, and Bhagat 2001; Sarathy 1990; Walters 1990). It substantively covers the key focus of the journal, i.e. international business and related works. This may be the reason for the development of the cluster in the initial years of the journal. However, the count of publications gradually declined after 1999. The cluster has had no publications in the most recent five years. The cluster credits 732 citations to the journal, which shows the prominence of the topics covered by it. The article titled ‘Mission Based Strategies for Internationalizing U.S Business Schools’ (Kedia and Cornwell 1994) is the most cited article of the cluster, followed by ‘Project-based Learning and International Business Education’ (2006), crediting 45 and 29 citations to the journal, respectively

Cluster 2, with 113 publications, focuses largely on the international business curriculum (Milhauser and Rahschulte 2010; Shooshtari and Manuel 2014). The cluster also covers themes like study abroad, global complexity, risk and curriculum internationalization (Presley, Damron-Martinez, and Zhang 2010; Relyea, Cocchiara, and Studdard 2008; Sánchez, Fornerino, and Zhang 2006). It credits the highest number of citations to the journal (TC: 826). The cluster began in 1993 with one publication: Amine (1993) focused on international business training. Until 2005, an average of one article each year appeared in the cluster. The cluster gained momentum in 2006 and, subsequently, most publications appeared in this cluster. In recent years, maximum JTIB publications represents this cluster. This signifies the popularity and importance of the International business curriculum and related themes among scholars of international business education research.

Cluster 3, with 92, publications talks mostly about experiential learning, technology, social media, on-line teaching, virtual design and pedagogy (Aggarwal 2011; Alon and Herath 2014; Barczyk and Duncan 2012; Paul and Mukhopadhyay 2005). The cluster marked its presence in 1993 and has shown substantial growth after 2001. It is the second most active cluster in recent times, after Cluster 2. This may be connected to the development of information technology and possibilities of e-learning in the recent two decades. Cluster 4 is the smallest cluster, with 87 publications crediting 392 citations to JTIB. The cluster primarily focuses on cross-cultural issues in international business education. The themes covered by the cluster include cross-cultural business, cross-cultural management, cross-cultural training, teaching ethics, ethical training, ethical sensitivity and worldmindedness (Douglas and JonesRikkers 2001). The cluster started developing at the inception of the journal and experienced active publications until 2007. From 2008 to 2019, only 5 articles appeared in the cluster. This signifies the shift of focus of international business education research from (Cluster 1) and cross-cultural issues (Cluster 4) to international business curriculum, global complexities (Cluster 2) and experimental learning and technology (Cluster 3). Douglas and Jones-Rikkers’s ‘Study Abroad Programs and American Student Worldmindedness: An Empirical Analysis’ (2001) is the influential work in the cluster, with 96 citations, followed by Larson and Schermerhorn’s ‘Revisiting a Theory-supported Approach to Teaching Cross-cultural Management Skills’ (1998).
